buildings.name: Pantheon of Agrippa
buildings.summary: Built by Agrippa in 27-25 BC in his third consulship as part of his monumentalisation of the Campus Martius, decorated with caryatids by Diogenes of Athens and bronze capitals of Syracusan bronze. Dio says Agrippa wanted to name it after Augustus and place his statue inside; refused, he put statues of Augustus and himself in the pronaos.

buildings.note: Form debated. Beltrami (1892-93) found remains he read as a T-shaped temple with a transverse cella 43.76 x 19.82 m facing SOUTH; the 1996-97 excavations under the portico showed the Agrippan building also faced NORTH, with a pronaos about 21 m wide, and La Rocca argues for a circular open precinct behind. Modelled as a north-facing (rot 356) rectangular temple with transverse cella on Beltrami's dimensions; treat as one hypothesis.

buildings.name: Pantheon (Hadrianic rotunda)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt from scratch under Hadrian (brick stamps of c. 114-126; perhaps begun under Trajan by Apollodorus) with Agrippa's inscription repeated on the frieze. A rotunda whose concrete dome spans 43.3 m, exactly equal to its height, open to the sky through an 8.9 m oculus, fronted by a porch of sixteen monolithic granite columns in three rows and a tall intermediate block. Hadrian held court here.

buildings.name: Santa Maria ad Martyres (Pantheon)
buildings.builderName: Pope Boniface IV with the emperor Phocas
buildings.summary: The emperor Phocas gave the Pantheon to Pope Boniface IV, who consecrated it on 13 May 609 (or 610) as the church of Santa Maria ad Martyres, bringing cartloads of martyrs' bones from the catacombs. buildings.name: Saepta Julia
buildings.builderName: planned by Julius Caesar; completed by Agrippa
buildings.summary: Caesar planned in 54 BC a marble voting enclosure a mile around; Lepidus continued it and Agrippa finished and dedicated it in 26 BC, adorned with marble tablets and paintings. A vast colonnaded court about 310 x 120 m, its long sides formed by the Porticus Argonautarum (west, by the Pantheon) and the Porticus Meleagri (east). As voting lost its meaning it served for gladiatorial shows, a naumachia under Augustus, and as a luxury market.

buildings.name: Baths of Alexander Severus (Thermae Alexandrinae)
buildings.summary: Rebuilt and enlarged by Severus Alexander in 227, who brought a new aqueduct (Aqua Alexandrina) to feed them; granite columns from them were used to restore the Pantheon's portico in the 17th century.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 393
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Thermae Neronianae / Alexandrinae
Ghini, Le terme Alessandrine nel Campo Marzio (1988)

buildings.name: Gymnasium of Nero
buildings.summary: Nero dedicated a Greek-style gymnasium in 60/61 with free oil for senators and knights; struck by lightning in 62, it burned down, and a bronze statue of Nero melted into a shapeless mass.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 393
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Thermae Neronianae / Alexandrinae
Ghini, Le terme Alessandrine nel Campo Marzio (1988)
buildings.note: Probably adjoining the baths; placed north of them. Form conjectural.

buildings.name: Stadium of Domitian
buildings.summary: Built by Domitian for the Greek athletic contests of his Capitoline Games (first held in 86): 275 x 106 m with a travertine arcaded facade in two orders and seats for about 30,000. Its arena survives as Piazza Navona, the curved north end and straight south end still legible in the square.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 366-367
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Colini, Stadium Domitiani (1943)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Stadium Domitiani
buildings.note: Axis measured on satellite imagery of Piazza Navona: bearing 176.6 from the curved north end toward the straight south end (schema stadium convention). Remains of the north curve visible at Via di Tor Sanguigna.

buildings.name: Stadium of Domitian (restored by Severus Alexander)
buildings.summary: Restored by Severus Alexander, who held gladiatorial games here while the fire-damaged Colosseum was being repaired. Constantius II admired it on his visit in 357. In the Middle Ages houses were built into its cavea, preserving its shape; the martyr Agnes was venerated in its arcades.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 366-367
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Coarelli, Rome and Environs: An Archaeological Guide (2007)
Colini, Stadium Domitiani (1943)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Stadium Domitiani

buildings.name: Odeum of Domitian
buildings.summary: A roofed hall for musical contests of the Capitoline Games, south of the Stadium. The curved facade of Palazzo Massimo alle Colonne follows its cavea.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 276
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Odeum
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Cavea curve under Palazzo Massimo on Corso Vittorio, with a cipollino column of the stage in Piazza de' Massimi to the north: the audience looked north (rot 357). Diameter ~90 m estimated from the curve; the Regionary capacity of 10,600 'loca' is unreliable.

buildings.name: Odeum of Domitian (completed by Apollodorus)
buildings.summary: Completed or rebuilt by Trajan's architect Apollodorus of Damascus; Ammianus lists it with the Pantheon and the Stadium among the wonders Constantius II saw in 357.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 276

buildings.name: Column of Marcus Aurelius
buildings.summary: A 100-foot spiral column of Luna marble, modelled on Trajan's, whose frieze narrates Marcus Aurelius' wars against the Marcomanni and Sarmatians (172-175), including the 'rain miracle'. Begun after his death in 180, it was finished by 193, when its custodian Adrastus was granted timber from the scaffolding to build himself a house beside it.

phases.t: begun after the death of Marcus

scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 95
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Columna Marci Aurelii Antonini
Scheid and Huet (eds), Autour de la colonne Aurelienne (2000)
buildings.note: Location from the monument in Piazza Colonna. Column 29.6 m (100 Roman feet) on a pedestal originally ~10 m high (now partly buried), total ~39.7 m plus the bronze statue. rot 86 (entrance side) is assumed.

buildings.name: Temple of Divus Marcus
buildings.summary: The Senate decreed a temple to the deified Marcus Aurelius with its own priesthood; it is thought to have stood west of his column.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 246
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Marcus, divus, templum
buildings.note: Site unknown; west of the column toward Montecitorio is the usual guess. Form invented.

buildings.name: Column of Antoninus Pius
buildings.summary: A plain monolith of red Aswan granite, 50 feet high, raised by Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus to Antoninus Pius and Faustina after his death in 161. Its marble pedestal, with the apotheosis of the imperial couple and the cavalry parade of the funeral games, was found in 1703 and is in the Vatican.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 94
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Columna Antonini Pii
buildings.note: Base found in 1703 in the garden of the Casa della Missione north-west of Montecitorio; shaft 14.75 m. Total height with statue estimated. Orientation of the inscribed face uncertain.

buildings.name: Ustrinum of Antoninus Pius
buildings.summary: The cremation precinct of Antoninus Pius and Faustina: a travertine enclosure with an iron railing around a central platform for the pyre, found with the column base in 1703.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 402
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Ustrinum Antoninorum
buildings.note: Placed just north of the column base; layout simplified.

buildings.name: Ustrinum of Marcus Aurelius (?)
buildings.summary: A second cremation enclosure of the same type found under Piazza del Parlamento in 1907, attributed to Marcus Aurelius or another Antonine.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 402
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Ustrinum (Marci?)
buildings.note: Attribution and exact position uncertain.

buildings.name: Arch of Claudius (Via Lata)
buildings.summary: The Senate's arch for Claudius' conquest of Britain, built in 51-52 where the Aqua Virgo crossed the Via Lata, so that the aqueduct ran through its attic. The inscription recorded the surrender of eleven British kings without loss.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 23
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Claudii (a. 51-52 d.C.)
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Remains found in Via del Corso at Piazza Sciarra; the arch spanned the road, rot = road bearing (347, measured on the modern Corso between Piazza Venezia and Piazza Colonna). Number of bays uncertain.

buildings.name: Arcus Novus
buildings.summary: A 'new arch' built by Diocletian over the Via Lata, probably for his vicennalia of 303-304, reusing Claudian reliefs (now in the Boboli Gardens and Villa Medici); demolished in 1491 when Santa Maria in Via Lata was rebuilt.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 26
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Novus
buildings.note: Position beside Santa Maria in Via Lata; form simplified.

buildings.name: Arch of Hadrian (?) on the Via Flaminia
buildings.summary: Two Hadrianic reliefs (an apotheosis of Sabina and an imperial address) later built into the Arco di Portogallo may come from an arch of Hadrian standing on this spot, or may have been brought from elsewhere.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 23
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Hadriani
buildings.note: Highly conjectural predecessor; included because the brief asks for the debated Arch of Hadrian.

buildings.name: Arco di Portogallo
buildings.summary: A late antique arch over the Via Flaminia beside the later Palazzo Fiano, decorated with two Hadrianic reliefs, demolished in 1662 by Alexander VII to widen the Corso. Its modern name comes from a Portuguese cardinal's palace nearby. It is sometimes called the Arch of Marcus Aurelius, since one view dates the arch or its reliefs to him.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 23
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Arcus Hadriani; Arco di Portogallo
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Spanned the Via Flaminia south of the Ara Pacis site; rot follows the road (~357 here). Construction date late antique (c. 350 assumed).

buildings.name: Campus Agrippae
buildings.summary: The park Agrippa laid out east of the Via Lata, opened to the people by Augustus in 7 BC with the Porticus Vipsania along its edge.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 65
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Campus Agrippae
buildings.note: Extent conjectural; the Temple of Sol later occupied its northern part.

buildings.name: Porticus Vipsania
buildings.summary: Begun by Agrippa's sister Vipsania Polla and completed by Augustus, it displayed Agrippa's great map of the world, drawn from his commentaries. Galba's soldiers were stationed in it in 69.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 319
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Porticus Vipsania
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
buildings.note: Along the east side of the Via Lata north of the Aqua Virgo arch (Martial's dripping arch); extent and form conjectural.

buildings.name: Altar of Providentia Augusta (?)
buildings.summary: An altar to the Providence of Augustus set up under Tiberius, at which the Arval Brethren sacrificed; the Arval acts locate it in the Campus Agrippae.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 323
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Providentia Augusta, ara
buildings.note: Placement within the Campus Agrippae is a guess; date c. AD 20 assumed.

buildings.name: Temple of Sol Invictus (Templum Solis)
buildings.summary: Aurelian's temple of the Unconquered Sun, built after his victory over Palmyra and dedicated on 25 December 274, filled with Palmyrene spoils and served by a new college of pontifices Solis. Wine for the plebs was stored in its porticoes.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 363-364
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Sol, templum
Hijmans, 'Temple and priests of Sol in the city of Rome', Mouseion 10 (2010)
buildings.note: Debated. The Regionary Catalogues put it in Regio VII (Via Lata). The preferred site is east of the Via Lata in the former Campus Agrippae around San Silvestro in Capite, where Renaissance drawings (Palladio and others) record a huge double precinct: an outer court with semicircular ends and an inner court with a round(?) temple. The older location on the Quirinal (Colonna gardens) is now assigned to Caracalla's Serapeum. Dimensions follow the drawings loosely; front toward the Via Lata (rot 266).

buildings.name: Obelisk of the Horologium (Solarium) Augusti
buildings.summary: An obelisk of Psammetichus II brought from Heliopolis and set up by Augustus in 10 BC, after the conquest of Egypt, as the gnomon of a great meridian (or sundial) in the northern Campus; Pliny says its gilded ball cast the shadow, but that the readings had gone wrong for some 30 years in his day. Now in Piazza di Montecitorio.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 190-191
Buchner, Die Sonnenuhr des Augustus (1982)
Heslin, 'Augustus, Domitian and the so-called Horologium Augusti', JRS 97 (2007)
Haselberger (ed.), The Horologium of Augustus: Debate and Context (JRA Suppl. 99, 2014)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
buildings.note: Found in 1748 (and partly in 1512) under houses north of Piazza del Parlamento; placed here per that find-spot. Shaft 21.79 m; pedestal and globe add ~8 m.

buildings.name: Meridian pavement of Augustus
buildings.summary: A travertine pavement with a bronze meridian line north of the obelisk on which the noon shadow marked the seasons and zodiac signs. Buchner reconstructed a full sundial grid some 160 m across, aligned so that on Augustus' birthday the shadow pointed to the Ara Pacis; later work (Heslin, Haselberger) favours a meridian line only.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 190-191
Buchner, Die Sonnenuhr des Augustus (1982)
Heslin, 'Augustus, Domitian and the so-called Horologium Augusti', JRS 97 (2007)
Haselberger (ed.), The Horologium of Augustus: Debate and Context (JRA Suppl. 99, 2014)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
buildings.note: Only the meridian with Greek inscriptions was found (Via di Campo Marzio 48), at the Flavian level. Extent here is a compromise and conjectural.

buildings.name: Meridian of the Horologium (Domitianic relaying)
buildings.summary: The meridian was relaid about 1.6 m higher, probably under Domitian; a stretch with bronze Greek letters naming the zodiac signs and the Etesian winds survives in a cellar at Via di Campo Marzio 48.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 190-191
Buchner, Die Sonnenuhr des Augustus (1982)
Heslin, 'Augustus, Domitian and the so-called Horologium Augusti', JRS 97 (2007)
Haselberger (ed.), The Horologium of Augustus: Debate and Context (JRA Suppl. 99, 2014)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
buildings.note: Date of relaying (Flavian) approximate.

buildings.name: Ara Pacis Augustae
buildings.summary: The Altar of Augustan Peace, decreed by the Senate on 4 July 13 BC on Augustus' return from Spain and Gaul and dedicated on 30 January 9 BC. A marble precinct carved with the procession of the imperial family, Aeneas, Tellus and acanthus scrolls, enclosing the altar where magistrates, priests and Vestals sacrificed yearly.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 287-289
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
Rossini, Ara Pacis (2006)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Pax Augusta, ara
buildings.note: Original site under Palazzo Fiano at Via in Lucina, just west of the Via Flaminia; reassembled in 1938 by the Mausoleum. Precinct 11.6 x 10.6 m, main door and stair on the west toward the Campus (rot 267), back door toward the Via Flaminia. As the ground rose, a retaining wall was built around it in the 2nd century.

buildings.name: Mausoleum of Augustus

params.pillars: bronze tablets of the Res Gestae at the entrance

buildings.summary: Begun by Octavian in 28 BC, after Actium, between the Via Flaminia and the Tiber: a huge drum 87 m across faced in travertine, carrying an earthen mound planted with evergreens and topped by a bronze statue of Augustus, about 42 m high. Marcellus was the first buried (23 BC); Augustus' ashes followed in AD 14, then the Julio-Claudians to Nerva. Bronze pillars at the entrance carried the Res Gestae.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 247-249
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
von Hesberg and Panciera, Das Mausoleum des Augustus (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Augusti
buildings.note: Centre from the standing ruin (Piazza Augusto Imperatore). Entrance on the south (rot 177, Campus grid). Upper reconstruction (stepped drums vs. tumulus) debated; height ~42 m.

buildings.name: Mausoleum of Augustus (plundered)

params.pillars: bronze tablets of the Res Gestae at the entrance

buildings.summary: The tomb is said to have been plundered by Alaric's Goths in 410 and its urns scattered; it decayed into a fortified mound of the Colonna in the Middle Ages.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 247-249
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
von Hesberg and Panciera, Das Mausoleum des Augustus (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Augusti
buildings.note: Plundering in 410 is traditional rather than securely attested.

buildings.name: Obelisk at the Mausoleum of Augustus (east)
buildings.summary: One of a pair of uninscribed granite obelisks flanking the entrance of the Mausoleum, now on the Esquiline (behind Santa Maria Maggiore, 14.75 m) and the Quirinal (14.64 m).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 247-249
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
von Hesberg and Panciera, Das Mausoleum des Augustus (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Augusti
buildings.note: Not mentioned by Strabo; probably added later, perhaps under Domitian (from = 90 assumed). Found near the entrance in 1519 and 1527.

buildings.name: Obelisk at the Mausoleum of Augustus (west)
buildings.summary: One of a pair of uninscribed granite obelisks flanking the entrance of the Mausoleum, now on the Esquiline (behind Santa Maria Maggiore, 14.75 m) and the Quirinal (14.64 m).
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 247-249
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
von Hesberg and Panciera, Das Mausoleum des Augustus (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Augusti
buildings.note: Not mentioned by Strabo; probably added later, perhaps under Domitian (from = 90 assumed). Found near the entrance in 1519 and 1527.

buildings.name: Ustrinum (Busta) of Augustus
buildings.summary: Strabo describes the place where Augustus' body was burned: an enclosure of white marble with an iron railing, planted inside with black poplars, in the middle of the Campus near the Mausoleum. Cippi of imperial family members cremated here were found in 1777 near San Carlo al Corso.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 247-249
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Haselberger et al., Mapping Augustan Rome (JRA Suppl. 50, 2002)
von Hesberg and Panciera, Das Mausoleum des Augustus (1994)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Augusti
Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 402
buildings.note: Placed east of the Mausoleum toward the Via Flaminia where the cippi were found.

buildings.name: Tomb of Aulus Hirtius
buildings.summary: The consul Hirtius, killed at Mutina in 43 BC, was given a public burial in the Campus Martius, an exceptional honour. His travertine tomb was found in 1938-40 beneath the courtyard of the Palazzo della Cancelleria beside the Euripus.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 354
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Under the Cancelleria courtyard; covered by the basilica of San Lorenzo in Damaso in late antiquity (end date assumed).

buildings.name: Tomb of Sulla
buildings.summary: Sulla was cremated and buried in the Campus Martius with an unprecedented funeral in 78 BC; his epitaph, which he wrote himself, said no friend ever outdid him in kindness nor enemy in harm. Caracalla restored the tomb.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 357
buildings.note: Site unknown; placed in the western Campus.

buildings.name: Tomb of Julia, daughter of Caesar
buildings.summary: When Julia, Caesar's daughter and Pompey's wife, died in childbirth in 54 BC, the people seized her body from the consuls and buried it in the Campus Martius. Caesar's pyre was prepared next to it in 44.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 353
buildings.note: Site unknown; placed in the northern Campus.

buildings.name: Tomb of C. Poplicius Bibulus
buildings.summary: A plebeian aedile's tomb granted by the Senate on public land at the start of the Via Flaminia, at the foot of the Capitoline; its travertine facade with pilasters and inscription still stands by the Vittoriano.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 352
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
buildings.note: Date early to mid 1st century BC. Facade faces west onto the ancient road.

buildings.name: Tomb of the Domitii (Nero's tomb)
buildings.summary: The family tomb of the Domitii Ahenobarbi on the Collis Hortulorum (Pincian), visible from the Campus; Nero's ashes were placed here in a porphyry sarcophagus with an altar of Luna marble, enclosed in Thasian marble.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 352
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Sepulcrum Domitiorum
buildings.note: Tradition puts it at the site of Santa Maria del Popolo, under the Pincian slope; form conjectural.

buildings.name: Terraces of the Gardens of Lucullus
buildings.summary: Lucullus spent his Asian fortune on terraced gardens on the Pincian slope facing the Campus, crowned by a great exedra and nymphaeum. Later owned by Valerius Asiaticus, whom Messalina drove to suicide to seize them.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 200
Broise and Jolivet, in Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horti Luculliani
buildings.note: Following Broise and Jolivet's reconstruction around Trinita dei Monti and Villa Medici: stepped terraces with a hemicycle (~80 m across) facing west. Dimensions approximate.

buildings.name: Terraces of the Gardens of Lucullus (imperial property)
buildings.summary: Messalina was killed in these gardens in 48 after her mock marriage to Silius; the estate passed to the emperors and later to the Acilii Glabriones.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 200
Broise and Jolivet, in Cima and La Rocca (eds), Horti Romani (1998)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Horti Luculliani

buildings.name: Mausoleum of Hadrian
buildings.summary: Hadrian's dynastic tomb across the Tiber in his family's gardens, linked to the Campus by the Pons Aelius: a square base about 89 m a side carrying a drum 64 m across and 21 m high, faced in Parian marble with statues, crowned by a smaller structure with a bronze quadriga. Completed by Antoninus Pius in 139; the emperors to Caracalla were buried in it.
scholarship: Richardson, A New Topographical Dictionary of Ancient Rome (1992) 249-251
Claridge, Rome (Oxford Archaeological Guide, 2nd ed. 2010)
Steinby (ed.), Lexicon Topographicum Urbis Romae (1993-2000), s.v. Mausoleum Hadriani
Pierce, 'The Mausoleum of Hadrian and the Pons Aelius', JRS 15 (1925)
buildings.note: Centre fitted to the drum on satellite imagery (Castel Sant'Angelo). Entrance toward the bridge, rot 177. Upper storey reconstruction debated; total height ~48 m.
